title: Best Gratitude Journal Apps in 2026: Honest Picks, Free and Paid
description: Best gratitude journal apps in 2026, honestly compared by use case — Gratitude: Self-Care Journal, Five Minute Journal, Day One, Presently and Thankful — on free tier, prompts, routines and looking back, checked against US App Store listings in November 2026.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

Comparison November 2026 · 9 min read By the Anicca Team

The best gratitude journal app in 2026 is the one that matches when and how you actually write. For a guided gratitude practice with prompts, affirmations and vision boards in one place, Gratitude: Self-Care Journal is the most complete option. For a fixed morning and evening routine, the Five Minute Journal is the most polished. If gratitude is one part of a bigger diary, Day One is the strongest long-term archive. For a completely free app on Android, Presently has no ads, no in-app purchases and nothing to upgrade. And for the smallest possible daily practice on iPhone — three things, written in your own words, next to a daily affirmation — that is the job Thankful is built for.

We reviewed the top gratitude journal apps available today — what each one does well, where each falls short, and which one is right for your practice.

We're going to be upfront: we make one of the apps on this list. Thankful is our app, and we obviously think it's good — but we also know it's not right for everyone. This comparison is our honest attempt to help you find the app that fits your actual practice, even if that app isn't ours. That is why our own app is listed last, not first, and why its limits are stated in the same format as everyone else's.

We evaluated each app on five factors: core features, how quickly you can start writing, prompts and guidance for blank days, pricing, and experience quality — including whether you can look back at old entries, which is where most of the good feeling in a gratitude practice actually comes from. Ratings, rating counts, versions and update dates below were checked against US App Store listings in November 2026. Here's what we found.

## The Apps, One by One

### Gratitude: Self-Care Journal

Best for: people who want the most guided gratitude practice

Gratitude: Self-Care Journal is the category leader this comparison is measured against, and it earns that position on depth. Alongside the daily gratitude journal itself, it offers hundreds of prompts and categories for blank days, photo and voice entries, daily affirmations, and vision boards. If you want gratitude to be the center of a wider self-care practice — journaling in the morning, an affirmation during the day, a vision board for where you're heading — this is the one app here that tries to hold all of that at once.

The tradeoff is size. If you only want to write three good things and close the app, this is a lot of app to walk past every evening, and the fuller experience sits behind its Pro tier. Checked in November 2026: Gratitude: Self-Care Journal is rated 4.9 from 45,002 ratings on the US App Store, version 6.0.4, last updated 22 November 2026 — the largest ratings base of any gratitude-specific app on this page, and the most recently updated, so it is actively maintained at a scale the rest of this list does not match.

**Strengths**

- Most complete gratitude-specific feature set here
- Hundreds of prompts, plus affirmations and vision boards
- Photo and voice entries, not just text
- 45,002 US ratings checked in November 2026, updated the same week

**Limitations**

- A lot of app if you only want three lines a night
- Extras sit behind the Pro tier
- Guided structure can crowd a simple practice

### Five Minute Journal

Best for: people who want a set morning and evening routine

The Five Minute Journal is the app version of the well-known paper journal, and it keeps the same fixed shape: in the morning you list three things you are grateful for, note what would make the day great, and write an affirmation; in the evening you record what went well. It is the most finished-feeling app on this list, and the free version is a complete journal with reminders and a passcode. Premium adds photos, custom questions, a mood tracker and an "On This Day" view of past entries.

The tradeoff is the routine itself. The questions are the same every day, which is exactly the point for people who thrive on a fixed ritual — and exactly the problem for people who start answering on autopilot by the third week. Checked in November 2026: 5 Minute Journal・Daily Diary is rated 4.8 from 17,637 ratings on the US App Store, version 4.3.31, last updated 9 November 2026.

**Strengths**

- Proven morning and evening structure
- Free version is a complete journal
- Reminders and passcode included
- Polished, calm design

**Limitations**

- Same questions every day can go stale
- Photos, custom questions and "On This Day" need Premium
- The routine asks for two sessions a day, not one

### Day One

Best for: people who want gratitude inside a bigger journal

Day One is not a gratitude app, and this page won't pretend otherwise. It is the best general journal on this list: multiple journals side by side, photos and other media in entries, a daily prompt and a prompt library that includes gratitude among many other topics, and a deep, searchable archive that rewards you years later. If you already keep a diary — or want one place for gratitude, travel, work notes and everything else — one app beats two.

The tradeoff is that gratitude is a guest in Day One, not the host. There is no gratitude-specific flow, and the free plan works on one device with limited media; syncing across devices needs the paid Silver plan, which is a lot to pay for three lines a night if gratitude is all you want it for. Checked in November 2026: Day One: Daily Journal & Diary is rated 4.8 from 119,077 ratings on the US App Store, version 2026.23, last updated 10 November 2026 — the biggest ratings base on this page by a wide margin.

**Strengths**

- Deepest, most searchable archive here
- Photos and media inside entries
- Daily prompt plus a broad prompt library
- 119,077 US ratings checked in November 2026

**Limitations**

- Not gratitude-specific; no guided gratitude flow
- Free plan is limited to one device
- Sync and full media need the paid plan

### Presently

Best for: people on Android who want a gratitude app that is actually free

Presently is the honest answer to "is there a gratitude app that's actually free?" It is deliberately plain: you open it, write what you are grateful for, and move on. Roundups consistently describe it as free with no ads and no in-app purchases, with entries kept on your phone rather than behind an account. For Android users who find that every other journal eventually asks for a subscription, that plainness is the whole appeal.

The tradeoff is availability, and it is a hard one: Presently is Android only. We checked the US App Store in November 2026 and there is no iOS listing for it, so there are no iPhone rating, version or update figures to report here — if you are on iPhone, this option simply does not exist for you yet, and the closest free-and-private pattern on iPhone is a minimal journal with no account, which is part of why we built Thankful the way we did.

**Strengths**

- Completely free, with nothing to unlock
- No ads and no account standing between you and writing
- Entries stay on your device
- Deliberately simple — fast to open, fast to finish

**Limitations**

- Android only; no iPhone or iPad version
- No US App Store listing to verify ratings or update history against
- Plain by design — no affirmations, vision boards or guided extras

### Thankful

Best for: people who want the smallest possible daily gratitude practice on iPhone

Thankful is our app, listed last because we publish this page. It is built around one small, repeatable rhythm: three numbered spaces to write what you noticed today, a daily affirmation on the same home screen to pause with, a calendar history so you can return to earlier entries by date, and a streak that shows the days you came back — without turning a missed day into another thing to feel bad about. Your day doesn't have to be extraordinary, and you don't need a polished story: a kind message, a quiet cup of coffee, something you finally finished. That is the size of entry Thankful is designed for, on iPhone and iPad. See how it works at https://aniccaai.com/thankful

The honest limits: Thankful is new and small. Checked in November 2026: Thankful - Gratitude Journal is version 1.0.3 on the US App Store, last updated 11 November 2026, and it has no US ratings yet — zero, against 45,002 for Gratitude and 119,077 for Day One above. It is free to download with optional Thankful Pro subscriptions; check the in-app purchase screen for current prices before subscribing, because we would rather you read them there than trust a number on a blog page. If you want hundreds of prompts, vision boards or a decade-deep archive today, the apps above are more proven. If you want three spaces, an affirmation, and a calendar of your own ordinary days, that narrow job is the one Thankful does.

**Strengths**

- Three spaces — the smallest daily commitment on this page
- Daily affirmation on the same screen as your journal
- Calendar history and streak, without streak guilt
- Free to download, no ads, iPhone and iPad

**Limitations**

- No US ratings yet — the least proven app on this page
- iPhone and iPad only; no Android version
- No prompt library, vision boards or photo journal
- Optional Thankful Pro subscription for the fuller experience

## How to Choose the Right App

The best gratitude journal app is the one you'll still be opening in March. A few questions that help narrow it down:

**Do you want guidance, or a blank space?** If blank pages stall you, Gratitude: Self-Care Journal's prompts and categories are the strongest support here. If prompts feel like homework, Presently on Android and Thankful on iPhone both start from the opposite premise: a small empty space and your own words.

**Do you want a fixed routine?** The Five Minute Journal is the only app here built around the same morning and evening questions every day. That sameness is a feature if ritual carries you, and a bug if repetition bores you.

**Is gratitude the whole practice, or one part of a bigger journal?** If it's one part, Day One's archive and media support win, and it isn't close. If gratitude is the whole practice, a gratitude-specific app will feel lighter every single night.

**What does "free" have to mean?** Presently is free with nothing to unlock, but Android only. Five Minute Journal's free version is a complete journal. Gratitude and Thankful are free to download with paid tiers behind them — read the purchase screen, not the blog post, before you decide.

**Can you look back?** Reading old entries is where most of the good feeling comes from. Day One is deepest here, Thankful keeps a simple calendar of your days, and every app on this list gives you some way back — check that the way back is one you'll actually use.

## Our Take

We built Thankful because the gratitude apps we kept opening asked for more than the moment had. A long entry, a library of prompts, a routine twice a day — all good things, and all easy to abandon on exactly the hard, ordinary days when noticing one good thing matters most. So Thankful asks for three things, in your own words, next to a daily affirmation, and keeps them on a calendar you can wander back through. Gratitude is one part of what we make at Anicca — a behavior intervention practice that also includes affirmations, manifestation and comedy — and you can compare that wider practice in our flagship roundup at https://aniccaai.com/blog/best-affirmation-apps-2026-11-05 and in today's companion comparison at https://aniccaai.com/blog/best-affirmation-apps-2026-11-24

We're obviously biased. But if you've tried gratitude apps before and quietly stopped opening them, the missing piece is probably not more features. It's a smaller promise — one you can keep on a bad day.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: What is the best gratitude journal app in 2026?**

A: It depends on when and how you write. For the most guided practice, Gratitude: Self-Care Journal is the strongest option. For a fixed morning and evening routine, the Five Minute Journal is the most polished. For gratitude inside a larger diary, Day One is best. For a completely free app on Android, Presently has nothing to unlock. For the smallest daily practice on iPhone, Thankful asks for just three things a day.

**Q: Are there gratitude journal apps that are completely free?**

A: Yes. Presently on Android is free with no ads and no in-app purchases. The Five Minute Journal's free version is a complete journal. Most other gratitude apps, including Gratitude: Self-Care Journal and our own Thankful, are free to download with optional paid tiers — check the in-app purchase screen for current prices.

**Q: What should I look for in a gratitude journal app?**

A: Speed first: if it takes more than a few seconds to start typing, you'll stop. Then prompts for blank days, a way to look back at old entries — that rereading is where much of the benefit sits — and honesty about what the paid tier actually adds. An app that guilts you about a streak is working against the practice it's supposed to support.

**Q: Is a gratitude app better than a paper journal?**

A: Neither, in general. A phone is always with you, so you can catch the good thing as it happens, and search or revisit it by date later. A notebook is quieter and asks nothing of you but the writing. The research is on the habit, not the tool: what matters is a few specific lines, a few times a week, kept up over months. The best app is simply the one that keeps that habit alive for you.
